paragraphs.text: Gongjian, the [tribute tip](anhua-dark:family), is one of the three loose tips of Anhua tea, lightly pressed into bamboo baskets rather than moulded into bricks or rolls. It sits in the middle of the three, between Tianjian above it and the coarser, stalkier Shengjian below, since the raw leaf is sorted into [numbered grades](anhua-dark:grades) and each tea is made from the grade that suits it. The loose tips grew out of the [Qing border trade](anhua-dark:history) to the north-west.

The leaf comes from Anhua County, a mountain county on the Zi river in Hunan and a protected origin for [Anhua dark tea](anhua-dark:definition). Like every Anhua tea it began as one raw tea, [heimaocha](anhua-dark:making): fixed, rolled, piled, rolled again and dried, then steamed soft and pressed lightly, as the loose tips are.

This is a 2024 tea, two years old. Anhua tea is [kept for years](anhua-dark:ageing) and said to improve as it rests, though no agreed count of years marks it as aged. Kept clean, dry and aired, away from other smells, it can be left to change over the years ahead.

brewing.text: In a small pot or gaiwan, use water at the boil and start with a steep of about 15 to 30 seconds, a little longer each round. Pressed and aged Anhua tea is also commonly simmered in a pot.

notice.text: Pine smoke or pine resin above all, a sweet taste and aftertaste, and a mellow, thick, smooth cup; a liquor from yellow and orange to orange-red. Young tea is often smokier in the first infusions and a little bitter, sweetening as the infusions go on.
